Urban planners increasingly promote mixed-use neighborhoods to reduce commuting time and improve community interaction. By placing housing, shops, offices, and public services within walking distance, cities aim to lower traffic congestion, reduce air pollution, and make daily life more convenient. Residents can access groceries, schools, and workplaces without long drives, which can save money and time. This model also supports local businesses because people are more likely to shop in nearby stores when they do not need to travel far.

Supporters argue that mixed-use development creates stronger communities. When people live, work, and spend leisure time in the same area, they are more likely to know their neighbors. This social connection can increase safety and encourage civic participation. Mixed-use planning often includes public spaces such as small parks, cafés, and community centers, which provide informal meeting points. These features make neighborhoods feel more welcoming and can improve overall quality of life.

However, critics raise several concerns. One issue is gentrification. When a neighborhood becomes more attractive, property values can rise, and long-term residents may be pushed out due to higher rents. Another concern is that mixed-use development can increase noise and reduce privacy, especially if residential areas are placed next to restaurants or entertainment venues. Critics also argue that not all neighborhoods have equal access to these investments, which can widen social inequality between districts.

Policy design therefore matters. Cities that want the benefits of mixed-use development must also create protections for affordability. Affordable housing programs, rent controls, or subsidies can help keep existing residents in place. Good zoning policies can balance commercial and residential needs by limiting noisy businesses in certain areas and requiring green buffers. Transportation planning also remains important, because mixed-use does not eliminate the need for public transit; it changes travel patterns rather than removing travel entirely.

Overall, mixed-use development offers clear advantages, but it is not a simple solution. It requires careful planning, transparency, and long-term community engagement. When designed responsibly, it can reduce congestion, support local economies, and create more connected neighborhoods. When designed poorly, it can increase inequality and social tension. The passage suggests that mixed-use planning is best seen as a tool that must be combined with social policy and consistent management.

Online education has expanded rapidly due to technological advances and changing expectations about how learning should occur. Many students appreciate the flexibility of online classes because they can study at their own pace and fit lessons around work or family responsibilities. For students in remote areas, online programs remove geographic barriers and allow access to universities that would otherwise be unreachable. Digital platforms also provide quick access to lecture recordings, notes, and discussion boards.

Despite these advantages, online education presents challenges. Some students struggle with motivation when learning alone, and they miss the structure of physical classrooms. Peer interaction can be weaker, which reduces opportunities for collaboration and informal learning. In addition, technical problems such as poor internet connectivity can interrupt learning. Teachers also face difficulties in evaluating participation and ensuring academic integrity when students are not physically present.

Hybrid models have emerged as a response to these challenges. In a hybrid system, students attend some classes in person while completing other activities online. This approach combines the flexibility of digital learning with the social benefits of face-to-face interaction. Students can build relationships with classmates during in-person sessions and then continue discussions online. Hybrid courses often include interactive projects, group assignments, and in-class workshops that develop communication skills.

However, hybrid models require careful planning. If schedules are inconsistent, students may become confused about expectations. Teachers must design courses so that online and in-person components support each other, rather than repeat the same content. Institutions also need to provide training for instructors who are adapting to new teaching technologies. Without this support, hybrid models may become inefficient or frustrating for both teachers and learners.

The passage concludes that online and hybrid education can improve access and flexibility, but only if they are managed thoughtfully. Technology alone does not guarantee success; effective learning depends on structure, interaction, and support. When institutions invest in guidance and clear expectations, online and hybrid systems can become sustainable options for modern education.

Renewable energy sources such as wind and solar power are critical to reducing dependence on fossil fuels. These sources produce far less pollution and can be replenished naturally. Many governments invest in renewables to reduce carbon emissions and meet international climate goals. Wind farms and solar panels are increasingly visible in both rural and urban areas, demonstrating a global shift in energy priorities.

A major challenge, however, is intermittency. Wind does not always blow, and sunlight is not constant. This means renewable energy production can fluctuate, while energy demand remains steady. When supply drops unexpectedly, power grids can become unstable. To solve this problem, energy storage technologies are essential. Advanced batteries, pumped hydro systems, and emerging innovations such as hydrogen storage allow surplus energy to be stored and used later.

Storage systems are expensive, and their development requires long-term investment. Critics argue that without sufficient storage, renewables cannot replace fossil fuels at a large scale. Supporters respond that storage costs are decreasing as technology improves and manufacturing expands. Additionally, smart grid technology can help manage energy demand by shifting use to times when renewable supply is high.

Policy also plays a role. Governments can encourage adoption through subsidies, tax incentives, and research funding. They can also modernize energy grids to handle decentralized energy production, since renewable energy often comes from many small sources rather than a few large plants. Public acceptance is important as well. Communities may resist wind farms or large solar projects due to concerns about landscape changes or local wildlife.

The passage suggests that renewables are essential but require coordination between technology, policy, and community engagement. Without storage and grid modernization, renewable energy systems remain fragile. With them, renewable energy becomes a reliable and scalable alternative.

Public libraries have evolved far beyond their traditional role of lending books. In many cities, libraries now function as community centers that offer digital access, workshops, and safe study spaces. This shift is especially important for students who lack quiet environments at home or reliable internet access. Libraries provide computers, databases, and free Wi-Fi, which help reduce educational inequality.

Libraries also support lifelong learning. Workshops on job applications, language skills, and digital literacy attract adults who wish to improve their qualifications. Reading clubs and public lectures bring residents together and strengthen social ties. During exam periods, libraries often extend their hours and become key spaces for focused study. These services position libraries as essential public institutions rather than optional cultural facilities.

Funding, however, is a major challenge. Many libraries face budget cuts, which reduce staff and limit operating hours. Without proper maintenance, physical spaces become less safe or appealing. Digital services also require ongoing investment in technology and training. Librarians must keep up with new tools and guide users in evaluating online sources. This workload increases even as budgets shrink.

To address these pressures, libraries increasingly form partnerships with schools, universities, and nonprofit organizations. These partnerships provide resources, volunteers, and expertise. Some libraries also develop community outreach programs, offering mobile services to neighborhoods without nearby branches. Such initiatives expand access and demonstrate the library’s value to the public.

The passage concludes that libraries remain essential in a digital society. They provide equitable access to knowledge, support community development, and offer safe spaces for learning. Social media platforms prioritize engagement because it drives advertising revenue and user retention. Algorithms are designed to show content that users are likely to react to, which often includes emotionally charged or controversial posts. While this design can increase time spent on platforms, it also influences how people consume information. Users may see a narrow range of views, reinforcing existing beliefs rather than encouraging balanced understanding.

This phenomenon is often called an echo chamber. In an echo chamber, users are surrounded by opinions that mirror their own, making alternative viewpoints seem less credible or even invisible. Over time, this can increase polarization and reduce the ability to engage in constructive debate. Researchers have found that people who primarily receive information through social media may overestimate the popularity of their own views because they rarely encounter opposing perspectives.

However, social media also has positive effects. It connects communities, allows rapid sharing of information, and gives voice to marginalized groups. During emergencies or political events, social platforms can mobilize support and spread important updates quickly. The challenge is to balance these benefits with the risks of misinformation and ideological isolation.

Digital literacy education is one proposed solution. When users understand how algorithms work, they can interpret information more critically and seek diverse sources. Platforms can also adjust their recommendation systems to promote credible information and reduce the spread of harmful content. Governments and civil society organizations may support these efforts through public awareness campaigns and policy guidelines.

The passage suggests that social media is neither entirely harmful nor entirely beneficial. Its impact depends on how it is designed and how users interact with it. Responsible use, transparency, and digital education are necessary to ensure that social media contributes positively to public discourse.

passages.title: Urban Heat and Public Health
passages.passage:
Cities tend to be warmer than surrounding rural areas, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dense construction materials absorb solar radiation during the day and release heat slowly at night, which keeps nighttime temperatures elevated. This pattern can increase energy use, worsen air quality, and raise health risks, especially for older adults and outdoor workers. Researchers have found that neighborhoods with less tree cover and more asphalt often experience the highest heat burden. These findings have led some cities to adopt mitigation strategies such as reflective roofing, expanded green spaces, and redesigned street layouts that improve airflow.

However, implementing these measures is not merely a technical challenge. Funding constraints, competing political priorities, and unequal distribution of green infrastructure can limit the effectiveness of heat‑reduction plans. Critics argue that policies sometimes prioritize commercial districts while leaving low‑income areas exposed. Supporters counter that early projects can demonstrate value and attract further investment. The debate therefore centers on how to design interventions that are both scientifically effective and socially equitable.

Recent studies also caution that short‑term temperature reductions may not be sufficient if regional climate trends continue to intensify. Adaptation, they suggest, should combine immediate cooling tactics with long‑term resilience planning, including housing standards and public health outreach.

Recent evidence extends the discussion. A mixed-methods study of 1,480 university students across four campuses reported that structured feedback and spaced practice were the strongest predictors of improvement, accounting for nearly 42% of the observed gains. However, the authors also warn of an implementation gap: policies may be well-designed but inconsistently applied at the classroom level. They recommend transparent criteria, short feedback cycles, and a minimum of two revision checkpoints for complex tasks.

passages.title: BUEPT Sample: THE ECONOMICS OF HAPPINESS
passages.passage:
For most of recorded history, the relationship between wealth and happiness seemed obvious: more money meant a better life. Richer people could afford better food, safer homes, superior healthcare, and more leisure. This intuition was partly correct but, as decades of research have revealed, dramatically incomplete. The relationship between income and happiness turns out to be considerably more complicated, shaped by factors such as comparison with others, adaptation, and the distinction between experiencing and evaluating one's own life.
In the early 1970s, economist Richard Easterlin identified a puzzle that has generated debate ever since. Comparing data from multiple countries, he found that wealthier nations were not consistently happier than poorer ones, and that within countries, increases in national income over time did not appear to produce corresponding increases in average happiness. This became known as the 'Easterlin Paradox.' One explanation is hedonic adaptation: people quickly adapt to improvements in their material circumstances and return to a baseline level of happiness. A significant pay raise produces initial elation, but within months the new income level becomes normal, and the emotional benefit fades. Another explanation is social comparison: people evaluate their income not in absolute terms but relative to those around them. If everyone becomes wealthier at the same rate, no one feels richer relative to their neighbors.
More recent research has complicated Easterlin's findings. A widely cited study by economists Angus Deaton and Daniel Kahneman found that emotional wellbeing — how happy people feel day-to-day — increases with income, but only up to a certain threshold. Beyond roughly $75,000 per year (in 2010 U.S. dollars), additional income appeared to have little further effect on emotional wellbeing. However, life satisfaction — how people evaluate their lives overall — continued to rise with income even beyond this point. This suggests that money may help people feel their lives are going well in an abstract sense without necessarily making their everyday emotional experience more joyful.
If income explains relatively little of the variance in happiness, what does? Research consistently points to strong predictors. Social relationships — the quality of connections with family, friends, and community — are among the most powerful. A Harvard study tracking hundreds of individuals across their adult lives found that the warmth of close relationships predicted not only happiness but also physical health in old age, far better than income or professional success. Meaningful work — providing a sense of purpose, competence, and autonomy — is another powerful predictor. Leisure activities that involve full engagement, what psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi called 'flow' states, produce more lasting happiness than passive activities like watching television, even when the latter feels more immediately appealing.
These findings have significant implications for public policy. If national income growth does not reliably translate into greater wellbeing, governments may be misallocating effort by focusing almost exclusively on economic growth. Several countries — most notably Bhutan, but more recently New Zealand, Scotland, and Iceland — have begun developing alternative national metrics that include measures of mental health, social connection, environmental quality, and leisure time alongside or in place of GDP. Critics argue that economic growth remains essential for meeting basic needs and that happiness-oriented policies risk being vague and unmeasurable. Advocates counter that continuing to treat GDP as the primary index of progress ignores the very things research shows matter most to human wellbeing.

passages.title: BUEPT Sample: THE PSYCHOLOGY OF PROCRASTINATION
passages.passage:
Procrastination is far more complex than simple laziness. Nearly everyone puts off tasks from time to time, but for a significant portion of the population, delay has become a chronic pattern. Research consistently shows that procrastination is not primarily about time management — it is about emotion management. When people encounter a task they find unpleasant, anxiety-provoking, or boring, the brain's impulse is to seek short-term relief, even at the cost of long-term consequences. This emotional avoidance, rather than poor organization or lack of intelligence, is what drives most habitual procrastinators.
Neuroscience has shed light on why some people procrastinate more than others. Studies using brain imaging have found that habitual procrastinators tend to have a larger amygdala — the brain region associated with processing emotions and detecting potential threats. When these individuals are confronted with a difficult task, the amygdala interprets it as a threat and sends signals to avoid it. At the same time, the connection between the amygdala and the part of the brain responsible for goal-directed behavior tends to be weaker in procrastinators, making it harder for them to override emotional impulses with rational intentions.
One of the most counterintuitive findings in procrastination research is that self-criticism actually worsens the problem rather than solving it. Many people believe that being hard on themselves after a procrastination episode will motivate better behavior in the future. In reality, the guilt and shame produced by self-criticism increase the emotional discomfort associated with the task, making the individual even more likely to avoid it next time. Studies at Carleton University found that students who forgave themselves after procrastinating on the first exam procrastinated significantly less on the second exam compared to those who did not. Self-compassion, it seems, breaks the cycle rather than enabling it.
A less obvious cause of procrastination is perfectionism. While the stereotype of a procrastinator is someone who is disorganized and careless, many procrastinators are, in fact, deeply invested in doing things well. The fear of producing work that falls short of their own high standards leads them to delay starting — and sometimes finishing — tasks altogether. (A) This type of avoidance is known as self-handicapping: by not starting, the individual can attribute any eventual failure to a lack of effort rather than a lack of ability. (B) Rather than reflecting disorganization, this behavior paradoxically stems from caring too much. (C) In a distorted way, procrastination becomes a strategy for protecting self-esteem. (D)
Research suggests several evidence-based strategies for overcoming procrastination. Breaking tasks into smaller, more manageable steps reduces the sense of overwhelm that triggers avoidance. Implementation intentions — specific plans that specify when, where, and how a task will be completed — have been shown to dramatically improve follow-through. Removing environmental temptations (such as turning off notifications) decreases the cognitive effort required to stay focused. Some researchers also recommend 'temptation bundling' — pairing an unpleasant task with something enjoyable, such as only listening to a favorite podcast while exercising. passages.title: DNA Fingerprinting (More to Read II)
passages.passage:
The characteristics of living organisms, including humans, are essentially determined by information contained within DNA inherited from parents. Organisms with different characteristics have different DNA sequences. DNA fingerprinting is a rapid way to compare DNA patterns between organisms.

Although DNA fingerprinting is highly powerful, nothing in science is one hundred percent guaranteed. In criminal investigation, a DNA match indicates a probability rather than absolute certainty. That probability can be extremely high, but it is still expressed statistically.

The probability of a DNA fingerprint belonging to a specific person must be high, especially in criminal cases, because the result may support guilt or innocence. This concern has led some legal systems to re-open past convictions when DNA evidence was later reanalyzed.

A DNA fingerprint differs from a conventional fingerprint in important ways. It is present in every cell, tissue, and organ of the body and cannot be altered by known treatments. It is now possible to test tiny biological samples, including hair or degraded matter, and obtain a DNA profile.

DNA databases have expanded in many places, and this has made matching faster. Police can compare crime-scene evidence with existing profiles, even when no local suspect has been identified yet. At the same time, some people argue that wider DNA collection may raise privacy concerns.

In a controlled trial, 32 instructors implemented a common protocol for feedback timing and language. The group using the protocol reduced misunderstanding errors by 19%, while the comparison group showed no significant change. The authors emphasize that consistency in feedback language, not volume, was the critical driver.

passages.title: BUEPT Sample: FOOD SECURITY AND CLIMATE CHANGE
passages.passage:
Global food security — the ability of all people at all times to access sufficient, safe, and nutritious food — rests on an agricultural system that is highly sensitive to climate conditions. Temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, and the frequency of extreme weather events all directly influence crop yields and livestock production. As climate change intensifies, altering these variables in ways that are both gradual and increasingly unpredictable, the agricultural systems on which billions of people depend face a range of interconnected challenges. The consequences are not distributed equally: the regions most vulnerable to climate-driven disruptions in food production are often the same regions that are already most food insecure and least equipped to adapt.
The relationship between temperature and crop yields is not simple. For some crops and in some regions, moderate warming may initially improve growing conditions — extending frost-free growing seasons in higher latitudes, for instance. However, the overall trend projected by agricultural scientists is deeply concerning. Research suggests that for every degree Celsius of warming beyond current temperatures, yields of major staple crops such as wheat, rice, and maize may decline by between 3 and 10 percent. Higher temperatures also increase rates of evaporation and crop water stress, making irrigation more necessary precisely in regions where water is already scarce. Meanwhile, elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide — the primary driver of warming — has a complex relationship with plant growth: while higher CO2 levels can stimulate plant growth under controlled conditions, field studies suggest the benefit is far smaller than laboratory experiments implied, and that increased CO2 also reduces the protein content of some staple crops.
Beyond gradual warming, the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events — droughts, floods, heatwaves, and storms — poses immediate and acute risks to food production. A single severe drought can devastate a regional harvest; flooding can destroy crops, contaminate water supplies, and damage transport infrastructure in ways that take years to repair. In 2010–2011, a combination of drought in Russia and floods in Australia and Pakistan contributed to a global spike in wheat prices that was linked to food insecurity and political instability across North Africa and the Middle East. Importantly, as supply chains have become more globally integrated, shocks in one region increasingly transmit rapidly to global food prices, meaning that a harvest failure in a major exporting country can affect food affordability in countries thousands of miles away.
Vulnerability to climate-driven food insecurity is shaped by a combination of geographic, economic, and political factors. Smallholder farmers in tropical and subtropical regions — who produce much of the food consumed in developing nations — are especially exposed, as these regions are projected to experience the most severe warming and changes in precipitation. Countries that are heavily dependent on food imports and lack the foreign exchange reserves to manage price volatility face particular risks. Urban populations in developing countries, who may spend 50 to 80 percent of their income on food, are disproportionately affected by price spikes caused by supply disruptions. In contrast, wealthier countries and wealthier households within all countries have greater capacity to absorb higher food prices and to shift to alternative food sources.
Responding to the threat of climate-driven food insecurity requires simultaneous action on multiple fronts. In the short term, strengthening social protection systems — food subsidies, cash transfers, and nutritional programs — can help the most vulnerable households weather supply disruptions. Over the longer term, investment in climate-resilient agriculture is essential: developing and disseminating drought-resistant crop varieties, improving water management, restoring degraded soils, and diversifying agricultural systems to reduce dependence on a small number of vulnerable staple crops. Reducing food loss and waste — currently estimated at around one third of global food production — represents another major opportunity. Ultimately, however, addressing food insecurity also requires addressing climate change itself: without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, the adaptive measures available to agricultural systems will be progressively overwhelmed by the scale of climate disruption.

To combat procrastination, psychologists recommend strategies that address underlying emotions. Breaking a daunting project into manageable micro-tasks can reduce feelings of being overwhelmed. Cities tend to be warmer than surrounding rural areas, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dense construction materials absorb solar radiation during the day and release heat slowly at night, which keeps nighttime temperatures elevated. This pattern can increase energy use, worsen air quality, and raise health risks, especially for older adults and outdoor workers. Researchers have found that neighborhoods with less tree cover and more asphalt often experience the highest heat burden. These findings have led some cities to adopt mitigation strategies such as reflective roofing, expanded green spaces, and redesigned street layouts that improve airflow.

However, implementing these measures is not merely a technical challenge. Funding constraints, competing political priorities, and unequal distribution of green infrastructure can limit the effectiveness of heat‑reduction plans. Critics argue that policies sometimes prioritize commercial districts while leaving low‑income areas exposed. Supporters counter that early projects can demonstrate value and attract further investment. The debate therefore centers on how to design interventions that are both scientifically effective and socially equitable.

Recent studies also caution that short‑term temperature reductions may not be sufficient if regional climate trends continue to intensify. Adaptation, they suggest, should combine immediate cooling tactics with long‑term resilience planning, including housing standards and public health outreach.

Universities that expanded online assessment during emergency periods often adopted algorithmic proctoring systems to deter cheating. These platforms typically combine webcam monitoring, keystroke logs, and identity checks, then assign a risk score for each exam session. Administrators argue that such tools preserve academic standards in large classes where manual review is impractical. They also note that proctoring logs can document irregular events, which appears to increase procedural consistency.

Yet measurement specialists caution that consistency should not be confused with validity. A system may flag movement, eye direction, or background noise with technical precision while still misclassifying honest behavior as suspicious. Students with unstable internet, shared living spaces, or disability related accommodations may trigger alerts more frequently for reasons unrelated to misconduct. If these false positives influence grades, the test could end up measuring students' circumstances as much as their knowledge.

Recent policy discussions therefore focus on proportional use. Instead of relying on automated flags as final evidence, institutions are experimenting with layered safeguards: shorter open-resource exams, random oral follow-ups, and transparent appeal channels. In this model, technology supports human judgment rather than replacing it. The central policy question is not whether integrity matters, but how to protect integrity without undermining fairness and construct validity.

Each year, millions of people visit places associated with death, suffering, and disaster — from Auschwitz concentration camp in Poland to Chernobyl in Ukraine, from Ground Zero in New York to the killing fields of Cambodia. This phenomenon has come to be known as 'dark tourism,' a term coined by researchers John Lennon and Malcolm Foley in their 1996 study. Though the idea of seeking out places of tragedy might seem morbid, scholars argue that the motivations of dark tourists are rarely straightforward — and almost never ghoulish. People visit these sites to learn, to pay respect, to grieve, to reflect on the fragility of human life, or simply to connect with a history they have only read about in books.
Dark tourism is not a modern invention. Pilgrimages to the sites of saints' deaths, public executions in medieval town squares, and battlefield tours following the Napoleonic Wars all represent early forms of what we now call dark tourism. What distinguishes contemporary dark tourism is scale and accessibility: the rise of affordable air travel and the internet has made it possible for millions of people to visit sites that were once remote or unknown. The commercialization that has accompanied this growth, however, has generated considerable controversy. When a site of mass tragedy becomes a heavily marketed tourist destination with gift shops, paid-for photographs, and online booking systems, legitimate questions arise about the line between commemoration and exploitation.
Research into the demographics and motivations of dark tourists has produced complex and sometimes surprising results. Studies consistently show that dark tourists are, on average, more educated than the general tourist population and that educational motivation is the most commonly cited reason for visiting. Many visitors report feeling that physical presence at a site conveys historical reality in a way that books or documentaries cannot. Survivors, descendants of victims, and members of communities affected by past events also form a significant portion of visitors to sites such as Auschwitz or Hiroshima — for these individuals, the visit is explicitly memorial rather than touristic in nature. However, research also identifies a smaller segment of visitors drawn by what scholars call 'morbid curiosity,' a fascination with death and disaster that is not primarily educational.
Perhaps the most debated aspect of dark tourism is its ethics. Critics argue that transforming sites of mass suffering into consumer experiences risks trivializing the events that took place there and commodifying human pain for profit. The proliferation of selfie-taking at sites such as Auschwitz and the sale of merchandise connected to historical atrocities have provoked particular outrage. (A) Site managers and scholars have increasingly developed codes of conduct for visitors, emphasizing respectful behavior, silence in certain areas, and the prohibition of photographs in others. (B) Proponents of dark tourism counter that these sites already exist and would deteriorate without the revenue that visitor numbers generate. (C) They also argue that witnessing places of tragedy fosters empathy, prevents the fading of historical memory, and may even contribute to conflict prevention. (D) The question, then, is not whether dark tourism should exist but how it should be managed.
The perspective of local communities surrounding dark tourism sites is often overlooked in academic debates. In Cambodia, many residents living near the Khmer Rouge killing fields have mixed feelings about the tourism that has developed around these sites. On one hand, the sites bring income to local guides, businesses, and cultural institutions. On the other hand, many survivors and their descendants feel discomfort at the sight of foreign visitors photographing mass graves with expressions of curiosity or excitement. Similar tensions exist near Ground Zero in New York, where some residents and victims' families have objected to what they perceive as the over-commercialization of a site of national grief. These perspectives suggest that the ethical dimensions of dark tourism cannot be resolved through academic debate alone — they require ongoing dialogue with the communities most directly affected.

passages.title: BUEPT Sample: The Ethics of AI in Healthcare
passages.passage:
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into healthcare promises to revolutionize medicine, from improving diagnostic accuracy to personalizing treatment plans. AI algorithms can analyze vast amounts of medical data far more quickly and accurately than human doctors, identifying patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed. However, the use of AI in clinical settings also raises significant ethical concerns, particularly regarding transparency, bias, and the potential for reduced human agency in medical decision-making.
Transparency, or the 'black box' problem, is a major ethical challenge. Many AI algorithms, particularly deep learning models, are highly complex, making it difficult for even their creators to understand how they arrive at a particular diagnosis or recommendation. This lack of transparency can undermine trust between patients and doctors, as patients may be hesitant to follow a treatment plan generated by a system they do not understand. Furthermore, if an AI system makes a mistake, it can be difficult to determine where the error occurred and who should be held accountable.
Bias in AI algorithms is another critical concern. AI systems are trained on historical medical data, which may contain biases reflecting existing inequalities in healthcare. If these biases are not identified and corrected, AI systems can perpetuate or even exacerbate health disparities. For example, an algorithm trained primarily on data from one demographic group may be less accurate when applied to individuals from other backgrounds. Ensuring that AI systems are trained on diverse and representative datasets is essential for achieving equitable healthcare outcomes.
Furthermore, the use of AI in medical decision-making raises questions about the role of human agency. While AI can provide valuable insights, it should not replace the clinical judgment and empathy of human doctors. There is a risk that doctors may become over-reliant on AI recommendations, leading to a 'deskilling' of the medical profession. Maintaining the 'human in the loop' is crucial to ensure that medical decisions are not only based on data but also consider the unique values, preferences, and circumstances of each patient.
In conclusion, the ethical integration of AI in healthcare requires a careful balance between innovation and responsibility. This involves developing 'explainable AI' that provides clear justifications for its recommendations, as well as establishing robust regulatory frameworks to ensure safety and accountability. Ultimately, AI should be seen as a tool to augment, rather than replace, human expertise, with the goal of improving health outcomes while upholding the core ethical principles of medicine: beneficence, non-maleficence, and respect for patient autonomy.

Almost everyone procrastinates occasionally, but chronic procrastination can severely impact academic and professional success. Procrastination is often misunderstood as simple laziness or a failure of time management. However, psychologists define it primarily as an emotional regulation problem. When individuals encounter a task that provokes anxiety, boredom, or feelings of incompetence, they defer the task to avoid those negative emotions in the short term.

This avoidance yields immediate relief but inevitably generates long-term stress. The 'procrastination cycle' begins with apprehension regarding a task, leading to delay. As the deadline approaches, anxiety intensifies, reducing the quality of work when the individual finally begins. Consequently, the individual associates the task with stress, reinforcing the desire to avoid similar tasks in the future.

To combat procrastination, psychologists recommend strategies that address underlying emotions. Breaking a daunting project into manageable micro-tasks can reduce feelings of being overwhelmed. Furthermore, practicing self-compassion rather than harsh self-criticism after procrastinating has been shown to decrease future delays. Recognizing that procrastination is an emotional response rather than an intellectual failure is the first step toward developing healthier productivity habits.

Urbanization is one of the most defining trends of the 21st century, with more than half of the world's population now living in cities. While urban living offers numerous economic and social opportunities, it also presents significant challenges for mental health. Research consistently shows that urban dwellers are at a higher risk for mental health disorders, such as anxiety and depression, compared to those living in rural areas. This 'urban penalty' is often attributed to a combination of environmental stressors, social isolation, and the fast-paced nature of city life.
One of the primary environmental stressors in cities is noise pollution. Constant exposure to traffic, construction, and high population density can lead to chronic stress and sleep disruption, both of which are major risk factors for mental illness. Additionally, the lack of green spaces and natural light in many urban environments can negatively impact mood and cognitive function. 'Biophilia,' the innate human tendency to seek connections with nature, is often stifled in modern cities, leading to a sense of disconnection and increased psychological distress.
Socially, cities can be paradoxically isolating. Despite the high density of people, urban environments often lack the close-knit social support systems found in rural communities. The transient nature of urban populations and the prevalence of single-person households can lead to feelings of loneliness and social fragmentation. Furthermore, the high level of social competition and the pressure to succeed in a competitive urban environment can exacerbate stress and feelings of inadequacy.
The fast-paced nature of city life also contributes to 'urban stress.' The constant demand for attention and the rapid influx of information can lead to cognitive overload and mental fatigue. This state of perpetual 'fight-or-flight' can drain mental resources and reduce an individual's resilience to stress. Psychologists argue that the 'always-on' culture of modern cities prevents individuals from having the necessary downtime for mental recovery and reflection.
To address these challenges, urban planners and policymakers must prioritize mental health in city design. This includes increasing the amount of green and blue spaces, reducing noise pollution, and creating environments that foster social connection and community. 'Healthy urbanism' advocates for cities that are designed with human needs in mind, promoting physical activity, social interaction, and access to nature. Ultimately, creating mentally healthy cities requires a holistic approach that recognizes the deep connection between our environment and our psychological well-being.

passages.title: BUEPT Sample: FOOD SECURITY AND CLIMATE CHANGE
passages.passage:
Global food security — the ability of all people at all times to access sufficient, safe, and nutritious food — rests on an agricultural system that is highly sensitive to climate conditions. Temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, and the frequency of extreme weather events all directly influence crop yields and livestock production. As climate change intensifies, altering these variables in ways that are both gradual and increasingly unpredictable, the agricultural systems on which billions of people depend face a range of interconnected challenges. The consequences are not distributed equally: the regions most vulnerable to climate-driven disruptions in food production are often the same regions that are already most food insecure and least equipped to adapt.
The relationship between temperature and crop yields is not simple. For some crops and in some regions, moderate warming may initially improve growing conditions — extending frost-free growing seasons in higher latitudes, for instance. However, the overall trend projected by agricultural scientists is deeply concerning. Research suggests that for every degree Celsius of warming beyond current temperatures, yields of major staple crops such as wheat, rice, and maize may decline by between 3 and 10 percent. Higher temperatures also increase rates of evaporation and crop water stress, making irrigation more necessary precisely in regions where water is already scarce. Meanwhile, elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide — the primary driver of warming — has a complex relationship with plant growth: while higher CO2 levels can stimulate plant growth under controlled conditions, field studies suggest the benefit is far smaller than laboratory experiments implied, and that increased CO2 also reduces the protein content of some staple crops.
Beyond gradual warming, the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events — droughts, floods, heatwaves, and storms — poses immediate and acute risks to food production. A single severe drought can devastate a regional harvest; flooding can destroy crops, contaminate water supplies, and damage transport infrastructure in ways that take years to repair. In 2010–2011, a combination of drought in Russia and floods in Australia and Pakistan contributed to a global spike in wheat prices that was linked to food insecurity and political instability across North Africa and the Middle East. Importantly, as supply chains have become more globally integrated, shocks in one region increasingly transmit rapidly to global food prices, meaning that a harvest failure in a major exporting country can affect food affordability in countries thousands of miles away.
Vulnerability to climate-driven food insecurity is shaped by a combination of geographic, economic, and political factors. Smallholder farmers in tropical and subtropical regions — who produce much of the food consumed in developing nations — are especially exposed, as these regions are projected to experience the most severe warming and changes in precipitation. Countries that are heavily dependent on food imports and lack the foreign exchange reserves to manage price volatility face particular risks. Urban populations in developing countries, who may spend 50 to 80 percent of their income on food, are disproportionately affected by price spikes caused by supply disruptions. In contrast, wealthier countries and wealthier households within all countries have greater capacity to absorb higher food prices and to shift to alternative food sources.
Responding to the threat of climate-driven food insecurity requires simultaneous action on multiple fronts. In the short term, strengthening social protection systems — food subsidies, cash transfers, and nutritional programs — can help the most vulnerable households weather supply disruptions. Over the longer term, investment in climate-resilient agriculture is essential: developing and disseminating drought-resistant crop varieties, improving water management, restoring degraded soils, and diversifying agricultural systems to reduce dependence on a small number of vulnerable staple crops. Reducing food loss and waste — currently estimated at around one third of global food production — represents another major opportunity. Ultimately, however, addressing food insecurity also requires addressing climate change itself: without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, the adaptive measures available to agricultural systems will be progressively overwhelmed by the scale of climate disruption.

Proponents of genetic engineering argue that parents should have the right to choose certain traits for their children, such as increased intelligence or physical prowess. However, critics warn that this could lead to a new form of eugenics, where social and economic inequalities are reinforced through genetic enhancement. Genetic engineering is a complex process, and unintended 'off-target' effects could lead to unforeseen health problems in future generations. The lack of consensus on the safety and efficacy of these technologies has led many scientists and ethicists to call for a global moratorium on germline editing until its implications are fully understood. The irreversibility of such changes means that we must proceed with extreme caution.
There are also concerns about the impact of genetic engineering on human diversity and our understanding of what it means to be human. By choosing certain traits and eliminating others, we risk narrowing the range of human variation. This could lead to a loss of the very diversity that has allowed our species to thrive and adapt. Additionally, the move toward genetic perfection could increase social pressure to conform to specific norms, further stigmatizing those with disabilities or 'non-ideal' traits.
In conclusion, while genetic engineering offers immense potential for medical advancement, it also presents significant ethical and social challenges. Navigating this new frontier requires careful consideration of the potential risks and benefits, as well as a robust public dialogue on the values we want to uphold. Ultimately, the future of genetic engineering should be guided by a commitment to justice, equity, and the preservation of human dignity for all.

groups.transcript:
Good afternoon, everyone. Today, we’re delving into the socio-spatial dynamics of the modern megacity, specifically focusing on the phenomenon of 'vertical urbanism.' As global populations continue to migrate toward urban centers, the traditional horizontal expansion—often termed 'urban sprawl'—has reached its ecological and logistical limits. In response, architects and urban planners have turned to the sky, creating hyper-dense, high-rise environments that promise efficiency but also pose significant challenges to social cohesion.

[Section 2] One of the primary criticisms of vertical living is what sociologists call 'social atomization.' In a traditional low-rise neighborhood, the street functions as a 'third space'—a communal area for spontaneous interaction. However, in a skyscraper, the common areas are often limited to elevators and corridors, which are transit zones rather than social ones. This lack of 'informal surveillance' and shared public space can lead to a sense of isolation among residents, despite the physical proximity of thousands of people. The 'vertical gated community' often exacerbates this by creating physical and psychological barriers between neighbors of different socio-economic backgrounds.

[Section 3] To combat this, some innovative designers are proposing 'vertical villages.' These are buildings that incorporate 'sky gardens,' communal kitchens, and multi-level plazas that function as artificial streets. The goal is to replicate the horizontal social dynamics within a vertical structure. For example, the 'Bosco Verticale' in Milan uses extensive greenery not just for environmental benefits—like air purification and temperature regulation—but to create a 'living' environment that encourages residents to spend more time in shared outdoor spaces. By 'interspersing' residential units with communal hubs, these designs aim to foster 'serendipitous' interactions that are the bedrock of community formation.

[Section 4] However, the success of these interventions often depends on 'socio-economic homogeneity.' When high-rise developments are segregated into luxury towers and low-income social housing, the vertical landscape becomes a physical manifestation of class division. This 'spatial segregation' is often reinforced by 'poor doors'—separate entrances for residents of subsidized housing—which further stigmatize lower-income individuals and prevent meaningful cross-class interaction. Therefore, the challenge for future urbanism is not just to build taller, but to build more 'inclusive' vertical communities that facilitate interaction across different demographic groups.

[Section 5] Another critical dimension is the 'environmental impact' of super-tall structures. While high density can reduce per-capita energy consumption by shortening travel distances and centralizing utilities, the embodied carbon of steel and concrete required for skyscrapers is immense. The 'stack effect'—the movement of air in and out of buildings due to air buoyancy—also presents significant challenges for heating and cooling. Modern 'smart skins'—facades that can adapt to changing weather conditions—are being developed to mitigate these issues, but the 'lifespan' of such high-tech solutions remains a topic of debate.

[Section 6] In Asia, cities like Hong Kong and Singapore have pioneered the 'Transit-Oriented Development' (TOD) model, where high-density residential towers are integrated directly with subway stations. This 'seamless' transition from home to work reduces reliance on cars and creates a highly efficient, albeit hyper-active, urban rhythm. However, critics argue that this 'efficiency-first' approach often comes at the cost of 'human scale' and 'psychological well-being.' The feeling of being 'submerged' in a forest of concrete can lead to chronic stress and a loss of connection to the natural world.

[Section 7] The role of 'public-private partnerships' in shaping vertical urbanism is also significant. In many cities, the 'skyline' is dictated by the profit motives of developers rather than the needs of the community. 'Bonus zoning'—where developers are allowed to build taller in exchange for providing public amenities—is a common tool used by city governments to fund infrastructure. However, the 'public' nature of these spaces is often questionable, as they are frequently managed by private security firms that restrict 'undesirable' activities and individuals.

[Section 8] From a psychological perspective, 'high-rise living' has been linked to various outcomes, particularly for children and the elderly. Studies have shown that children living on higher floors have fewer opportunities for outdoor play, which can affect their motor development and social skills. For the elderly, the 'barrier' of the elevator can lead to increased sedentary behavior and a heightened risk of social isolation. Designing 'age-friendly' vertical environments requires a rethink of how we allocate space for multi-generational activities.

[Section 9] The concept of the 'vertical farm' is perhaps the most futuristic adaptation of this model. By integrating hydroponic and aeroponic systems into urban towers, we could potentially grow food within the very centers where it is consumed. This would significantly reduce the 'food miles' and environmental footprint of our agricultural systems. While still in its nascent stages, vertical farming represents a potential path toward 'urban self-sufficiency' in an era of climate uncertainty.

[Section 10] Ultimately, the future of vertical urbanism will be determined by our ability to balance 'efficiency' with 'empathy.' As we continue to build upward, we must ensure that our towers are not just 'machines for living'—as Le Corbusier once famously described them—but vibrant, inclusive, and sustainable communities. This requires a 'holistic' approach to design that prioritizes the human experience over architectural spectacle. The skyscraper of the future must be more than a landmark; it must be a home.

passages.passage:
For most of recorded history, the relationship between wealth and happiness seemed obvious: more money meant a better life. Richer people could afford better food, safer homes, superior healthcare, and more leisure. This intuition was partly correct but, as decades of research have revealed, dramatically incomplete. The relationship between income and happiness turns out to be considerably more complicated, shaped by factors such as comparison with others, adaptation, and the distinction between experiencing and evaluating one's own life.
In the early 1970s, economist Richard Easterlin identified a puzzle that has generated debate ever since. Comparing data from multiple countries, he found that wealthier nations were not consistently happier than poorer ones, and that within countries, increases in national income over time did not appear to produce corresponding increases in average happiness. This became known as the 'Easterlin Paradox.' One explanation is hedonic adaptation: people quickly adapt to improvements in their material circumstances and return to a baseline level of happiness. A significant pay raise produces initial elation, but within months the new income level becomes normal, and the emotional benefit fades. Another explanation is social comparison: people evaluate their income not in absolute terms but relative to those around them. If everyone becomes wealthier at the same rate, no one feels richer relative to their neighbors.
More recent research has complicated Easterlin's findings. A widely cited study by economists Angus Deaton and Daniel Kahneman found that emotional wellbeing — how happy people feel day-to-day — increases with income, but only up to a certain threshold. Beyond roughly $75,000 per year (in 2010 U.S. dollars), additional income appeared to have little further effect on emotional wellbeing. However, life satisfaction — how people evaluate their lives overall — continued to rise with income even beyond this point. This suggests that money may help people feel their lives are going well in an abstract sense without necessarily making their everyday emotional experience more joyful.
If income explains relatively little of the variance in happiness, what does? Research consistently points to strong predictors. Social relationships — the quality of connections with family, friends, and community — are among the most powerful. A Harvard study tracking hundreds of individuals across their adult lives found that the warmth of close relationships predicted not only happiness but also physical health in old age, far better than income or professional success. Meaningful work — providing a sense of purpose, competence, and autonomy — is another powerful predictor. Leisure activities that involve full engagement, what psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi called 'flow' states, produce more lasting happiness than passive activities like watching television, even when the latter feels more immediately appealing.
These findings have significant implications for public policy. If national income growth does not reliably translate into greater wellbeing, governments may be misallocating effort by focusing almost exclusively on economic growth. Several countries — most notably Bhutan, but more recently New Zealand, Scotland, and Iceland — have begun developing alternative national metrics that include measures of mental health, social connection, environmental quality, and leisure time alongside or in place of GDP. Critics argue that economic growth remains essential for meeting basic needs and that happiness-oriented policies risk being vague and unmeasurable. Advocates counter that continuing to treat GDP as the primary index of progress ignores the very things research shows matter most to human wellbeing.

passages.title: BUEPT Sample: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND THE FUTURE OF WORK
passages.passage:
Automation has reshaped the economy before. The industrial revolution replaced artisans with machines; the mechanization of agriculture displaced millions of farm laborers; the spread of computers in the late 20th century transformed office work beyond recognition. Each of these transitions produced short-term disruption and long-term structural change, and each generated its own wave of anxiety about the future of human employment. The emergence of modern artificial intelligence — capable of performing not just routine physical and clerical tasks but complex cognitive work such as image recognition, legal analysis, medical diagnosis, and creative content generation — has reawakened this anxiety with unprecedented intensity.
Current AI systems excel at a specific set of tasks. They are extraordinarily good at recognizing patterns in large datasets — far faster and more accurately than any human. This capability makes them highly effective at a wide range of applications: diagnosing diseases from medical images, detecting fraud in financial transactions, filtering spam, translating languages, and generating text that is indistinguishable from that produced by a human writer. They are also effective at optimization — finding the most efficient solution to a well-defined problem — which makes them valuable in logistics, manufacturing scheduling, and resource allocation. Critically, these capabilities are not limited to manual or low-skill work: many high-skill, well-paid professional tasks are also vulnerable to automation.
Despite these capabilities, current AI systems have significant limitations. They struggle with tasks that require genuine common-sense reasoning, physical dexterity in complex and unpredictable environments, deep empathy, and ethical judgment. Jobs that combine these qualities — skilled trades such as plumbing, electrical work, and surgery; care-based professions such as nursing, social work, and early childhood education; and roles requiring creative leadership and interpersonal trust — have proven more resilient to automation than many economists initially predicted. AI systems are also brittle in the face of novelty: they perform well within the boundaries of the data they were trained on but can fail unpredictably when confronted with genuinely new situations.
The economic impact of AI-driven automation is unlikely to be evenly distributed. Research by economists Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo suggests that the adoption of industrial robots has depressed wages and employment for workers in affected industries, with limited evidence of compensating job creation in other sectors. Workers without post-secondary education — those most likely to hold automatable jobs — face the greatest risk of displacement. Geographically, regions whose economies depend heavily on manufacturing and routine service work face more severe impacts than economically diverse urban centers. These distributional effects raise serious concerns about widening inequality, as the gains from automation accrue primarily to the owners of capital and to highly skilled workers whose expertise complements AI, while the costs fall disproportionately on those with the least capacity to adapt.
There is no consensus on how best to respond to the challenges posed by AI-driven automation. Some economists and technologists are optimistic: they argue that, as in previous technological transitions, new forms of work will emerge to replace those lost, and that the net effect of AI on employment will be positive. Others are more skeptical, pointing out that the pace of this transition may outstrip the ability of educational systems and labor markets to adapt. Policy proposals range from investment in education, retraining programs, and lifelong learning infrastructure, to more radical ideas such as robot taxes — levies on the use of automation that would fund social support systems — and universal basic income schemes that would provide all citizens with a minimum income regardless of employment status. What seems clear is that the social consequences of AI-driven automation will be shaped not only by the technology itself, but by the political choices societies make about how to manage and distribute its effects.

passages.title: BUEPT Sample: SLEEP DEPRIVATION AND COGNITIVE PERFORMANCE
passages.passage:
In many parts of the world, insufficient sleep has become so normalized that people wear it as a badge of pride. 'I only need five hours,' is the kind of boast one hears in competitive professional environments. Yet the scientific consensus is unambiguous: almost no one functions well on five hours, and virtually no one is genuinely immune to the cognitive consequences of sleep loss. The assumption that sleep deprivation is a minor inconvenience — something that coffee and willpower can overcome — is not just incorrect; it is demonstrably dangerous.
Sleep plays a crucial role in the formation and consolidation of memory. During sleep — particularly during the slow-wave and REM stages — the brain replays and organizes the information it encountered during waking hours, transferring it from short-term into long-term memory. People who sleep after learning new material retain significantly more than those who remain awake. A single night of poor sleep before an exam can reduce recall ability by up to 40%, according to studies at the University of California, Berkeley. Crucially, a well-rested brain also takes in new information more effectively, suggesting that sleep functions both before and after learning to maximize retention.
Beyond memory, sleep deprivation severely impairs decision-making, particularly the ability to assess risk. Studies consistently show a pattern researchers call 'optimism bias under fatigue': exhausted people tend to underestimate dangers and overestimate their own abilities. (A) This is especially concerning in high-stakes environments. (B) Research on medical professionals found that doctors working shifts longer than 24 hours make significantly more diagnostic errors. (C) One landmark study found that surgical residents on such shifts made 36% more serious medical errors than those on shorter schedules. (D) Data from the US Centers for Disease Control indicates that drowsy driving causes around 72,000 crashes and 800 deaths every year.
Chronic sleep deprivation — consistently sleeping fewer than the recommended seven to nine hours — does not merely affect mental performance. Over time, it disrupts hormonal balance, suppresses immune function, increases inflammation, and raises the risk of Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and obesity. Sleep-deprived individuals produce more ghrelin (which signals hunger) and less leptin (which signals satiety), leading to increased caloric intake. In studies where participants slept only six hours per night for two weeks, their cognitive performance declined to the equivalent of two full nights without sleep — yet the participants themselves reported feeling only slightly impaired, revealing a worrying lack of self-awareness about their actual functioning.
Public health experts recommend consistent sleep schedules, limiting screen exposure before bed, keeping bedrooms cool and dark, and avoiding caffeine after midday. At the institutional level, several US high schools have experimented with later start times for teenagers, whose circadian rhythms shift during adolescence to favor later sleep and waking. passages.title: BUEPT Sample: THE SCIENCE OF BOREDOM
passages.passage:
Boredom has long been dismissed as a trivial emotional state — the minor irritation of a restless mind with nothing to do. In recent years, however, psychologists and neuroscientists have begun to study it more seriously, revealing it to be a remarkably complex and consequential experience. Boredom is now understood not merely as the absence of stimulation, but as an active state in which the mind is searching for meaning and engagement it cannot find. This distinction matters because it shifts the question from 'How do we stop being bored?' to 'What is boredom trying to tell us?'
Research has established a useful distinction between two forms of boredom: state boredom and trait boredom. State boredom is situational — it arises from a specific environment or task that offers insufficient stimulation, and it passes when the situation changes. Trait boredom, on the other hand, is a relatively stable personality characteristic: some individuals are chronically prone to boredom regardless of their circumstances. These individuals report lower life satisfaction, are more likely to engage in risk-taking behavior, and are at greater risk of depression and substance abuse than those who rarely experience boredom. However, researchers caution that the relationship may be mediated by third factors such as difficulty with self-regulation.
One of the more counterintuitive findings in boredom research is that boredom may have significant creative benefits. Studies by Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman found that participants who performed a boring task — copying out a phone book — subsequently showed greater creativity on divergent thinking tasks than a control group. The researchers proposed that boredom triggers the mind to wander in search of stimulation, and that mind-wandering activates what neuroscientists call the 'default mode network' — brain regions associated with daydreaming, imagination, and loose associative thinking underlying creativity. This suggests that immediately reaching for a phone at the first sign of boredom may be counterproductive, effectively short-circuiting a mental process with real cognitive value.
Despite its potential benefits, chronic boredom has serious negative consequences. Studies have linked it to overeating, excessive social media use, impulsive spending, and aggressive behavior. In occupational settings, boredom at work — sometimes called 'boreout,' in contrast to 'burnout' — leads to disengagement, absenteeism, and reduced productivity. Importantly, workplace boredom does not stem exclusively from tasks that are too simple; it can also arise when tasks are too complex and overwhelming, when workers lack clear goals, or when they feel their skills are being wasted. This complexity means that solutions must be more sophisticated than simply making jobs more challenging.
Perhaps the most philosophically interesting question raised by boredom research is what boredom reveals about the human need for meaning. Existentialist philosophers such as Martin Heidegger argued that profound boredom — the kind that strips away all distractions — forces the question of what one genuinely values. Modern psychologists have found empirical support for this view: studies show that individuals who tend to experience boredom as deeply aversive also score lower on measures of meaning in life and are more likely to describe their existence as purposeless. In this sense, boredom may function as an emotional signal — not simply an unpleasant state to be escaped, but a prompt to examine whether one's life is genuinely aligned with one's values.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, how has the scientific understanding of boredom changed in recent years?

passages.title: BUEPT Sample: THE PSYCHOLOGY OF PROCRASTINATION
passages.passage:
Procrastination is far more complex than simple laziness. Nearly everyone puts off tasks from time to time, but for a significant portion of the population, delay has become a chronic pattern. Research consistently shows that procrastination is not primarily about time management — it is about emotion management. When people encounter a task they find unpleasant, anxiety-provoking, or boring, the brain's impulse is to seek short-term relief, even at the cost of long-term consequences. This emotional avoidance, rather than poor organization or lack of intelligence, is what drives most habitual procrastinators.
Neuroscience has shed light on why some people procrastinate more than others. Studies using brain imaging have found that habitual procrastinators tend to have a larger amygdala — the brain region associated with processing emotions and detecting potential threats. When these individuals are confronted with a difficult task, the amygdala interprets it as a threat and sends signals to avoid it. At the same time, the connection between the amygdala and the part of the brain responsible for goal-directed behavior tends to be weaker in procrastinators, making it harder for them to override emotional impulses with rational intentions.
One of the most counterintuitive findings in procrastination research is that self-criticism actually worsens the problem rather than solving it. Many people believe that being hard on themselves after a procrastination episode will motivate better behavior in the future. In reality, the guilt and shame produced by self-criticism increase the emotional discomfort associated with the task, making the individual even more likely to avoid it next time. Studies at Carleton University found that students who forgave themselves after procrastinating on the first exam procrastinated significantly less on the second exam compared to those who did not. Self-compassion, it seems, breaks the cycle rather than enabling it.
A less obvious cause of procrastination is perfectionism. While the stereotype of a procrastinator is someone who is disorganized and careless, many procrastinators are, in fact, deeply invested in doing things well. The fear of producing work that falls short of their own high standards leads them to delay starting — and sometimes finishing — tasks altogether. (A) This type of avoidance is known as self-handicapping: by not starting, the individual can attribute any eventual failure to a lack of effort rather than a lack of ability. (B) Rather than reflecting disorganization, this behavior paradoxically stems from caring too much. (C) In a distorted way, procrastination becomes a strategy for protecting self-esteem. (D)
Research suggests several evidence-based strategies for overcoming procrastination. Breaking tasks into smaller, more manageable steps reduces the sense of overwhelm that triggers avoidance. Implementation intentions — specific plans that specify when, where, and how a task will be completed — have been shown to dramatically improve follow-through. Removing environmental temptations (such as turning off notifications) decreases the cognitive effort required to stay focused. Some researchers also recommend 'temptation bundling' — pairing an unpleasant task with something enjoyable, such as only listening to a favorite podcast while exercising. The key insight is that fighting the behavior with willpower alone is rarely effective; instead, restructuring the environment and reframing the emotional relationship with tasks produces more lasting change.

answer: Paragraph 3 — The student's cycle of guilt after procrastinating and then repeating the behavior matches the paragraph's argument that self-criticism increases avoidance and perpetuates the pattern.

answer: Willpower alone is rarely effective because it does not address the emotional and environmental factors that trigger avoidance. Restructuring the environment and reframing one's emotional relationship with tasks produces more lasting change.

groups.transcript:
[Introduction]
Boğaziçi University, Writing and Academic Support Center, selective listening. Urban Psychology: The Impact of City Architecture on Human Behavior.

The topic of today's lecture is the invisible force that shapes our daily lives. The point in question is urban psychology. Today, I am going to talk about how the physical architecture of our cities—the streets, the buildings, and the public spaces—dictates human behavior and community relations.

For many years, architects believed that a building's only purpose was to provide shelter and look aesthetically pleasing. However, modern environmental psychology measures these structures differently. Today, researchers study city layouts to understand how space influences human emotion. When people navigate through chaotic, noisy, and overcrowded city environments, they experience intense mental fatigue. Urban sociologists use a specific term to describe this phenomenon; they call it urban cognitive overload. If a city desires to maintain a healthy population, planners must find ways to reduce this constant psychological stress.

[The 1970s Housing Experiment]
Let me now explain how poor architectural design can actively destroy communities. In the 1970s, a massive public housing experiment was conducted in the United States, involving the construction of enormous high-rise apartment blocks. At first, authorities believed that the rising crime rates in these buildings were due to poverty or lack of police presence. However, architectural researcher Oscar Newman found something else. He discovered that the specific environmental factor that led to a significant drop in community trust was the lack of shared communal spaces. Because there were no courtyards or safe playgrounds where neighbors could naturally meet and talk, people became isolated and fearful of one another.

[Safety and 'Eyes on the Street']
Now, I'd like to talk about the concept of urban safety. How do we design safe neighborhoods? You might expect that the answer lies in installing thousands of security cameras or increasing police patrols. However, the famous urbanist Jane Jacobs proposed a completely different approach known as the "eyes on the street" theory. According to Jacobs, the primary architectural tool used to naturally reduce neighborhood crime is front-facing windows. When buildings are designed so that residents can easily look out onto the street from their living rooms or shops, criminals feel constantly watched. This natural surveillance is much more effective than artificial security measures.

[Social Infrastructure: Third Places]
There is yet another matter to be discussed: social infrastructure. Sociologists divide our living spaces into three categories. The "first place" is the home, which provides rest. The "second place" is the workplace or school, which demands productivity. But a healthy city desperately needs "third places," such as local cafes, public libraries, or neighborhood parks. Unlike homes or offices, third places primarily provide unplanned social interactions. These are neutral grounds where people of different social classes and backgrounds can interact without any obligations, fostering a strong sense of civic equality.

[Biophilic Design]
Now let us examine a modern architectural movement that aims to heal the urban mind. As cities became concrete jungles, rates of depression and anxiety skyrocketed. In response, architects developed a strategy called "biophilic design." The core principle of biophilic design is integrating nature into the built environment. This goes beyond just planting a tree on a sidewalk; it involves using natural light, flowing water features, and organic materials inside office buildings and hospitals to subconsciously connect humans with the natural world, which significantly lowers blood pressure and stress.

[Demographic Shifts]
However, despite these modern improvements, many mega-cities are currently facing a crisis. Are people still willing to live in these massive urban centers? While older generations often migrate to rural areas seeking peace and quiet, a recent demographic survey revealed a surprising shift among the youth. When asked why they are relocating to smaller towns, young professionals have increasingly cited extreme housing costs, long commute times, and a lack of green spaces. While career opportunities in big cities continue to be attractive, these negative lifestyle factors are driving the current urban exodus.

[Pedestrian Behavior]
Before we conclude, let me give you a brief, fascinating fact about pedestrian behavior. The architecture of a city literally dictates how fast you walk. Have you ever noticed that you walk much faster in a crowded metropolis than you do in a small town? Researchers have observed that pedestrians unconsciously synchronize their walking speed with the crowd around them. Social scientists refer to this phenomenon as the social contagion of pace. In dense urban areas, the collective anxiety and rush of the crowd physically transfer to the individual.

[Conclusion]
To conclude, I would like to emphasize that a city is not just a collection of concrete, steel, and glass; it functions very much like a living organism. If the buildings are the bones of the city, and the electrical grids are the nervous system, then the public transportation network is compared to the cardiovascular system. Just as veins and arteries pump blood to keep the body alive, a well-designed transit system pumps people, energy, and life into every neighborhood. When it clogs or fails, the entire organism suffers.

This ends my lecture. Thank you for your attention.
